questions.prompt: Put the browser request lifecycle in order.
questions.explanation: A browser first resolves the hostname, establishes a secure connection when using HTTPS, sends the request, then receives status, headers, and body.

concept_panel.title: DNS Resolution
concept_panel.explanation: DNS turns a human-readable domain into the IP address a client can connect to. It happens before the HTTP request is sent, so DNS failures look like connection failures rather than application bugs. In interviews, DNS is usually part of the browser-to-server lifecycle. The important mental model is that naming, connection setup, HTTP, and application logic are separate stages.
key_takeaways: DNS resolves names before HTTP starts.
DNS problems can prevent any request from reaching the server.
Caching can make DNS behavior look inconsistent during changes.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand the web request lifecycle below application code.
concept_panel.practical_example: A browser cannot call https://api.example.com until api.example.com resolves to an address.

questions.prompt: Which fields are usually part of an HTTP request?
questions.explanation: Requests contain routing and intent data: URL, method, headers, query parameters, and sometimes a body.

concept_panel.title: HTTP Request and Response
concept_panel.explanation: HTTP is a request-response protocol. The client sends a method, URL, headers, and sometimes a body; the server returns a status code, headers, and response body. Interview questions often test whether you can separate intent from outcome. Methods express what the client wants; status codes express what happened.
key_takeaways: Headers carry metadata for auth, content type, caching, and negotiation.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can reason about client-server contracts instead of memorizing codes.
concept_panel.practical_example: GET /users/7 asks for a resource; 404 says that resource was not found.

questions.prompt: Match the method to its normal intent.
questions.explanation: HTTP methods communicate intent. PATCH is partial update; PUT is full replacement; POST usually creates or triggers processing.

concept_panel.title: PATCH vs PUT
concept_panel.explanation: PUT normally means replacing the whole resource representation. PATCH means applying a partial update to selected fields. If the client only sends a new email, PATCH communicates the intended change without implying that omitted fields should be cleared. This is a contract question: the method should match the update semantics.
key_takeaways: PUT is full replacement in conventional REST design.
Choosing the right method prevents accidental data loss.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand API semantics and resource-update contracts.
concept_panel.practical_example: PATCH /users/5 with {"email":"new@example.com"} updates only the email field.

questions.prompt: A client sends only a new email for an existing user. Which method is most precise?
questions.explanation: PATCH communicates partial update. PUT would normally mean replacing the full user representation.

questions.prompt: Match each status code to the interview meaning.
questions.explanation: 401 is about missing/invalid authentication. 403 is about authorization after identity is known.

concept_panel.title: HTTP Status Codes
concept_panel.explanation: Status codes are compact signals about request outcomes. 2xx means success, 4xx means the client request has a problem, and 5xx means the server or dependency failed. The common interview trap is 401 vs 403: 401 means authentication is missing or invalid, while 403 means identity is known but access is denied.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can communicate API failures clearly to clients.
concept_panel.practical_example: A logged-in user without admin permission should usually receive 403, not 401.

questions.explanation: Headers are request/response metadata. Authorization, Content-Type, Accept, and Cache-Control are common HTTP headers.

questions.prompt: Your React app at localhost:5173 calls an API at localhost:8000 and the browser blocks it. What is the likely mechanism?
questions.explanation: Different scheme/host/port combinations are different origins. Browsers require the API to allow the frontend origin via CORS.

concept_panel.title: CORS and Origins
concept_panel.explanation: CORS is a browser security mechanism for cross-origin requests. An origin is the scheme, host, and port together, so localhost:5173 and localhost:8000 are different origins. The browser blocks the response unless the API explicitly allows the frontend origin. CORS does not protect server-to-server calls; it is enforced by browsers.
key_takeaways: Origin means scheme plus host plus port.
Browsers enforce CORS; servers declare allowed origins.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand browser security boundaries.
concept_panel.practical_example: A Vite frontend on localhost:5173 needs the FastAPI server on localhost:8000 to allow that origin.

concept_panel.title: Cookies and Sessions
concept_panel.explanation: Cookies are small values stored by the browser and sent with matching requests. Sessions usually store user state on the server and use a session ID in a cookie to link the browser to that state. This distinction matters for security and scaling. The cookie is not the whole user record; it is usually a pointer or token.
key_takeaways: Sessions usually live on the server.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand state in stateless HTTP workflows.
concept_panel.practical_example: A server stores cart state by session ID, while the browser only stores the session cookie.

questions.prompt: What does HTTPS add over plain HTTP?
questions.explanation: HTTPS uses TLS to protect confidentiality, verify the server identity, and detect tampering.

concept_panel.title: HTTPS and TLS
concept_panel.explanation: HTTPS is HTTP carried over TLS. TLS encrypts traffic, authenticates the server, and protects message integrity. This matters because tokens, cookies, and private payloads can otherwise be read or modified in transit. A strong answer separates transport security from application authorization.
key_takeaways: TLS does not replace input validation or authorization.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand transport security and where it sits in the request path.
concept_panel.practical_example: A login cookie sent over plain HTTP can be stolen by a network observer.

questions.prompt: A production site sends login tokens over plain HTTP. What is the bug?
questions.explanation: Without HTTPS, intermediaries may inspect or alter sensitive traffic such as tokens and session identifiers.
options: Traffic can be read or modified in transit
questions.answer: Traffic can be read or modified in transit

coding_challenges.title: Web Fundamentals status classifier
coding_challenges.instructions: Implement classify_status_code(code: int) -> str. Return success for 200-299, redirect for 300-399, client_error for 400-499, server_error for 500-599, and unknown otherwise.
coding_challenges.explanation: The challenge reinforces deterministic branching, status-code categories, and local test execution.
